rows.speaker: ulemâ
rows.claim: Some scholars who deny that the Prophet ever acted by independent judgment infer that position from this passage.
rows.anchor: ulemâ, bu âyet ile istidlâl etmişlerdir.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse at 9:43 and similar passages indicate that the Prophet exercised judgment, with mistaken judgment corrected by revelation.
rows.anchor: gibi âyetler Peygamber’de de ictihâdın vukū‘unu, ancak isabet olmazsa o hâlde bırakılmayıp vahiyle tashih edildiğini iş‘âr eder.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage primarily concerns the Qur'an; if extended to all the Prophet's speech, including hadith, it should be understood with regard to its ultimate outcome.
rows.anchor: Bu âyet de esas itibariyle Kur’an hakkında olmak gerektir.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present-tense form of revelation reinforces its confirmation and description, and hints at the preceding qualification of the Prophet's speech.
rows.anchor: وَحْىٌۭ يُوحَىٰ’da “vahy”in muzâri‘sîgasıyla tekid olunarak tahkik ve tavsîfinde buna da bir işaret yok değildir.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because taught takes two objects, one is omitted: either the Prophet is the object and Qur'an is implicit, or Qur'an is the object and the Prophet is implicit; the sense is the same.
rows.anchor: Tâlim etti ona “tâlim” fiili iki mef‘ûle ta‘addî eder. Bundan burada ya birinci veya ikinci mef‘ûlün mahzuf olduğunu anlarız.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is unquestionably the Qur'an's teacher, while Gabriel is the messenger who, by God's permission, brought and conveyed it to Muhammad's heart.
rows.anchor: Kur’ân’ı tâlim eden Allah teâlâ olduğunda şüphe yok ise de

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas identifies the one described as strong in powers as God.
rows.anchor: İbn Abbas’tan vârid olan bir rivayete göre Allah teâlâ denilmiş ise de

rows.speaker: Hazret-i Âişe
rows.claim: Aisha's report identifies Gabriel; many commentators prefer Gabriel because the wording and attributes suit him.
rows.anchor: Hazret-i Âişe’den vârid olan rivayette Cebrâil diye tefsir olunmuş ve evsâf ve elfâzın zâhiri de buna münâsib bulunmuş olduğundan çokları Cebrâil demişlerdir.

rows.speaker: Beyzâvî
rows.claim: Beyzavi calls him an angel of great powers, Gabriel, who mediates the manifestation of miracles.
rows.anchor: Beyzâvî مَلَكٌ شَدِيدٌ قـُوَاهُ وَهُوَ جَبـْرَائِيلُ فَإن َّهُ الْوَاسِطَةُ فِي إِبْدَاءِ الْخَوَارِقِ

rows.speaker: Taberî
rows.claim: Tabari glosses strong in powers as strong in means or resources.
rows.anchor: Taberî, “şedîdü’l-kuvâ, şedîdü’l-esbâb demektir” diyor.

rows.speaker: Nîsâbûrî
rows.claim: Nishaburi understands the phrase to mean that all of Gabriel's intellectual and practical powers are strong.
rows.anchor: Nîsâbûrî de “yani ilmî ve amelî kuvveleri hepsi şedîd” diye ifade etmiş

rows.speaker: Nîsâbûrî
rows.claim: Nishaburi says praising the teacher highlights the pupil's excellence; the wording also rebuts claims that a human taught him, since humans are weak and have little knowledge.
rows.anchor: Müte‘allimin fazileti anlaşılmak için muallim medholunmuştur.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mirra can mean gall, reason, strength, a turn, or firmness; accordingly possessor of mirra can describe force, intelligence, or a sound body.
rows.anchor: “murûr”un binâ-i nev‘i, öd, akıl, kuvvet, kat, sağlamlık gibi birkaç mânaya gelebileceğine göre

rows.speaker: müfessirîn
rows.claim: Commentators give three chief senses: strong; well-built and handsome; or, in Kashshaf, Baydawi, and Abu Suud, firm and incisive in judgment. The first can describe God, while the latter two suit Gabriel.
rows.anchor: müfessirîn başlıca üç mâna göstermişlerdir: 1. Kuvvetli 2. Sağlam yapılı, güzel manzaralı 3. Keşşâf, Beyzâvî ve Ebussuud’un ifadelerine göre akıl ve re’yinde hasâfet ve metânet sâhibi.

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Raghib distinguishes istiwa as equality between parties from istiwa describing a thing's balance, uprightness, or elevation; with ala it implies mastery.
rows.anchor: Râgıb der ki: “‘İstivâ’ kelimesi iki türlü kullanılır. Birisinde iki veya daha ziyade fâile isnad olunur;

rows.speaker: müfessirîn
rows.claim: Commentators differ whether the pronoun refers to Gabriel, the teacher, or to the Prophet, the pupil; on the Gabriel reading, the clause through 53:10 explains his teaching.
rows.anchor: Müfessirînin birkaç vechi vardır. Evvelâ bunun zamirinde iki vecih muhtemildir.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation says Gabriel appeared directly at the highest horizon in his true created form, rather than in a human guise; Muhammad saw him in that form twice, unlike other prophets.
rows.anchor: düpedüz kendi suretiyle ufuk-ı a‘lâda

rows.speaker: Bazıları
rows.claim: Other reported readings say Gabriel taught and then stood in heaven, or that he took control by his power in response to a command.
rows.anchor: Bazıları “tâlim etti de semâda durdu” demişler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalili prefers the Prophet as the subject: after Gabriel taught him, Muhammad rose and attained steadiness in knowledge and prophethood at the highest horizon.
rows.anchor: İstivâ eden Peygamber olduğuna göre ise -ki biz bu mâna üzerine yürümek istiyoruz-

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ufuq basically means an edge or boundary, especially the sky's rim; astronomical horizons are technical versions of the boundary between earth's plane and sky.
rows.anchor: “Ufuk” esas mânasında mutlaka kıyı ve kenar demektir. Bilhassa semânın kenarlarından kıyısına ve eteğine denir.

rows.speaker: Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: Razi reports the common view that Gabriel is the subject at the eastern horizon, but says the apparent intended subject is Muhammad, whose elevation is rank and status rather than physical location.
rows.anchor: Râzî der ki: “Meşhuru bu هَوَىٰ zamiri Cibrîl’indir.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One derivation links tadalla to dalal/tadallul: displaying charm or coquettish openness; ascribed to God, this could metaphorically express love manifesting between beloved and lover.
rows.anchor: Birisi “delâl”den aslı “tedellül” olarak dilber, naz suretinde cilve ve inbisat göstermektir.

rows.speaker: Bazıları
rows.claim: A second derivation takes tadalla from the yāʾ-root dalā, meaning to approach and humble oneself, making it a gloss on “he approached.”
rows.anchor: İkincisi: yâî olarak “delâ”dan yaklaşmak ve tevazu eylemek mânasına gelir ki burada bazıları bu mânayı vermişlerdir.

rows.speaker: müfessirîn
rows.claim: A third derivation takes it from the wāw-root dalw, bucket: the verb can mean letting something hang down or drawing it up, and many explain Gabriel's act as descending toward the Prophet.
rows.anchor: Üçüncüsü vâvî olarak “delv”den müştak olmasıdır. “Delv” ismi kofa demek olduğu gibi “delv” masdarı da kofayı sarkıtmak veya çekmek mânalarına geldiği için

rows.speaker: çokları
rows.claim: On the common Gabriel interpretation, he descended toward the Prophet after appearing at the highest horizon; this describes the first revelation in Hira but not the Prophet's ascent in the Mi'raj.
rows.anchor: çokları Cibrîl’in fiili olmak üzere sarkmak mânasıyla tefsir etmişlerdir.

rows.speaker: Beyzâvî
rows.claim: Those who take the approach and hanging as God's acts interpret the latter as drawing the Prophet in his entirety to the Holy Presence.
rows.anchor: Beyzâvî bunu naklederken وَتَدَل ِّيهِ جَذْبُهُ بِشَرَاشِرِهِ إلَى جَنَابِ الْقُدْسِ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalili reads the Prophet's state as the effect of divine attraction: he was drawn upward toward God's nearness beyond the highest horizon, signaling the Mi'raj; the servant's approach through supererogatory worship is thereby realized.
rows.anchor: Fakat biz bunu cezb değil cezbin eseri ve istivâ gibi Peygamber’in vasfı olmak üzere aynı mânadan incizab ile bir terakki anlıyoruz

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qaws is a bow; qab can name the spans between its grip and string, and some read two qabs of a single bow by metathesis.
rows.anchor: mâlum ki yay demektir. “Kāb” da yayın kabzasıyla

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas
rows.claim: In the Hijaz dialect qaws can mean a cubit; Ibn Abbas is reported to understand the phrase as about two cubits.
rows.anchor: Hicaz lügatında “kavs” zirâ‘mânasına geldiği ve İbn Abbas’tan burada bu mânaya olduğu da söylenmiştir.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalili prefers the alliance ritual: Arabs joined two bows at their qab, drew them together, and shot one arrow as an irrevocable pact of shared consent and anger, expressing exceptional and spiritual nearness.
rows.anchor: Araplar câhiliyede bir ittifak için antlaşacakları zaman iki yay çıkarır, birini diğerinin üzerine koyarak ikisinin kābını birleştirir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here qab depicts the two bows joined rather than a measurement; aw/adna advances to “even closer,” while the apparent alternative marks the description as figurative.
rows.anchor: “hatta daha yakın” mânasına bir terakki ifade eder. Böyle muhatabların bakımından terdid suretinde anlatılması da ifadenin temsîlî olduğunu ihtar içindir.

rows.speaker: müfessirîn
rows.claim: Exegetes say the representation of perfect nearness confirms that the Prophet heard the revelation, excluding distance that would obstruct contact.
rows.anchor: Bunun için müfessirîn derler ki kemâl-i kurbü tasvir eden bu ifade meleke-i ittisâli temsil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “His servant” refers to God in every reading, since God is understood from the preceding discussion even when the strong one is taken as Gabriel.
rows.anchor: عَبْدِهِۦ’deki zamirin Allah’a râci‘olduğunda ihtilâf yoktur. “Şedîdü’l-kuvâ”dan murad Allah teâlâ olduğuna göre bu zâhirdir.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading has Gabriel approach and convey each revelation God sent to Muhammad, first appearing in full form to establish its divine origin and then conveying it piecemeal.
rows.anchor: Cebrâil böyle yaklaştı da Allah’ın kulu Muhammed aleyhisselâm’a gönderdiği her vahyi getirdi, vahyetti onu öyle tâlim etti

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalili prefers that Muhammad, God's chosen servant, drew near to his Lord after the ascent and received revelation directly, without Gabriel as intermediary.
rows.anchor: Allah’ın has kulu olan sâhibiniz Muhammed aleyhisselâm o istivâdan sonra Rabbine öyle yaklaştı

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The well-known direct revelation at the Mi'raj was prayer; another report says no prophet or community will enter Paradise before Muhammad's prophet and community.
rows.anchor: Bunun birisi namaz olduğu mâruftur, bir de şu rivayet edilmiştir: Peygamberlerden hiçbiri senden evvel cennete girmeyecek

rows.speaker: Resûlullah
rows.claim: Muslim reports that the Prophet received five daily prayers and the closing verses of al-Baqara, and that grave sins were forgiven for community members who did not associate partners with God.
rows.anchor: Sahîh-i Müslim’de “Resûlullah’a üç şey verildi. Beş vakit namaz verildi, Sûre-i Bakara’nın havâtimi verildi

rows.speaker: Nizameddin Nîsâbûrî
rows.claim: Nishaburi says the revelation's details in that private gathering were apparently secrets, realities, and kinds of knowledge known only to God and His Messenger.
rows.anchor: Nitekim Nizameddin Nîsâbûrî tefsirinde der ki:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “what he saw” can refer to the servant or the heart; because 53:17 speaks of the eye, the sight was visual, and the heart's attestation shows that the vision and Mi'raj manifestations were real rather than imagined.
rows.anchor: رَأَىٰٓ zamiri “abd”e de “fuâd”a da gidebilir. مَا زَاغَ ٱلْبَصَرُ buyurulmasına göre bu rü’yetin basarî olması iktizâ eder.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's heart and conscience testified to what his powers saw, so he recognized Gabriel whenever he came, in whatever form.
rows.anchor: yalan çıkarmayıp şehadet ederek tasdik eylediği hakikattir. Onun için Cibrîl her geldikçe herhangi surette olursa olsun tanıdı.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present tense in “he sees” indicates continuing vision, and the following oath explicitly confirms that the Prophet saw him again.
rows.anchor: Muzâri‘sîgasıyla يَرَىٰ buyurulması rü’yetin istimrârına delâlet eder.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet saw Gabriel, the strong one and possessor of mirra, again in his true form during the descent from the Mi'raj; this indicates Gabriel's rank was below the Prophet's.
rows.anchor: Bir de o gördüğü Şedîdü’l-kuvâ Zû-mirre’yi, yani hakīkī sureti ve bütün kuvâsı ve kuvveti ile kendini tâlim eden Cibrîl’i bir de Mi‘râc’dan inerken gördü.

rows.speaker: müfessirînin çoğu
rows.claim: Most commentators parse nazlatan, as a once-form verbal noun, as an adverb meaning “on another occasion, in a descent.”
rows.anchor: Müfessirînin çoğu diyorlar ki: نَزْلَةً masdar binâ-i merre

rows.speaker: Hûfî ve İbn Atıyye
rows.claim: Hufi and Ibn Atiyya instead treat nazlatan as a verbal noun in circumstantial position, meaning “while descending.”
rows.anchor: ve İbn Atıyye gibi bazıları da hâl mevkiinde masdar olduğunu söylemişlerdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the adverbial reading, ukhra qualifies nazla as another descent; on the circumstantial reading it means another time, or modifies ra'a as another vision.
rows.anchor: أُخْرَىٰ evvelkine göre نَزْلَةً’in sıfatı, “diğer bir iniş”, ikinciye göre de مَ َّرةً أُخْرَى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators agree this descent took place on the Mi'raj night but differ over whose descent it was.
rows.anchor: Bu inişin Mi‘râc gecesi olduğunda ittifak vardır.

rows.speaker: Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: Razi rejects physical motion or descent for God; spiritual descent means approaching the servant with mercy and favor. He reads Moses' request as asking God to remove veils of majesty and approach graciously so he may see.
rows.anchor: Râzî der ki: “Allah teâlâ hakkında hareket ve nüzul tasavvuru bâtıldır. Manevî kurb ile nüzul ise rahmet ve fazl ile abdine yaklaşır da abd onu görmez.

rows.speaker: birçokları
rows.claim: Many identify the descending figure as Gabriel in his true form.
rows.anchor: Birçokları Cibrîl’in hakīkī sureti ile nüzûlü demişlerdir.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalili rejects Gabriel as the descending figure because Gabriel cannot pass the Sidra, so the location beside it does not fit a descent by him from above.
rows.anchor: Lâkin Cibrîl Sidre-i Müntehâ’dan öte geçemediğine göre

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalili takes it as the Prophet's descent from the Mi'raj, following the report that Gabriel stopped short because he would burn if he came a fingertip closer, while the Prophet passed beyond and Gabriel later returned to meet him.
rows.anchor: Râzî ve Nîsâbûrî’nin kaydettikleri vechile Mi‘râc haberlerinde vârid olduğuna göre Mi‘râc gecesi Cibrîl

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet went up and down several times when prayer was prescribed, so “another descent” aptly denotes the final descent; he saw Gabriel in assumed form at Qur'anic revelations and in true form once before and once during the Mi'raj return.
rows.anchor: Resûlullah namaz emrinde birkaç kereler inip çıkmış idi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sidrat al-Muntaha is a genitive construction; muntaha can be a place noun or a mim verbal noun, meaning the sidra at the final limit or of the ultimate boundary.
rows.anchor: “Sidre-i Müntehâ”, Müntehâ Sidresi, terkîb-i izâfîdir. “Müntehâ” ism-i mekân ve masdar-ı mîmî olabileceğine göre

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Kāmus entry identifies sidr as the nabq or Arabian cherry tree, lists its plurals and distinguishes garden and wild varieties, with sweet versus tart fruit and dense, pleasant shade.
rows.anchor: sîn’in kesri ve dâl’in sükûnuyla şecer-i nebk ismidir ki ‘Arabistan kirazı’ tâbir olunur. Trabzon hurması ol nevidendir.

rows.speaker: müfessirîn
rows.claim: Seder can mean dazzlement or bewilderment, and sidra as a noun of type can suggest astonishment; commentators use this alongside the tree sense.
rows.anchor: “Seder” ve “sederât” göz kamaşmak ve hayran olmak demektir.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The popular account places the tree at the right of the Throne in the seventh heaven, though a hadith says the sixth; rivers of the Paradise promised to the pious flow beneath it.
rows.anchor: Sidre-i Müntehâ, Arş’ın sağından yedinci semâda -bir hadiste de altıncı semâda- bir nebk ağacıdır

rows.speaker: Resûlullah
rows.claim: Prophetic reports describe a tree whose shade a rider could traverse for seventy years, or in another version a hundred, and whose leaf could cover the entire community.
rows.anchor: Hazret-i Peygamber’den bunun vasfında “nebkı

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalili sees the tree as an image of the created world's ultimate formation, marking the boundary of formed bodies and dimensions where the realm of command begins.
rows.anchor: Bunda bütün âlem-i halkın ecrâm ve eb‘âdı ile müntehâ-yı teşekkülâtı, âlem-i emir hudûduna dikilmiş bir ağaç

rows.speaker: İbn Mes‘ûd
rows.claim: Ibn Masud describes the Sidra at Paradise's extremities, with hems of fine silk and brocade over it; Kashshaf accordingly calls it at Paradise's end.
rows.anchor: Mes‘ûd radıyallâhu anh’tan da: الْجَن َّةِ عَلَيـْهَا فُضُولُ

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Ka'b say the Sidra is beneath the Throne, where knowledge of every angel, prophet, and other creature ends; what lies beyond is known only to God.
rows.anchor: İbn Abbas ve Ka‘b’dan nakledildiğine göre Sidre-i Müntehâ Arş’ın tahtında bir sidredir ki gerek melek ve gerek nebî

rows.speaker: Dahhâk
rows.claim: Dahhak's reported view is that every matter from the divine command reaches the Sidra and goes no farther.
rows.anchor: emr-i ilâhîden her şey ona müntehî olur. Ondan ileri geçmez.

rows.speaker: Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: Razi records an alternative that sidra is a noun of one occurrence from rider/rikba, so the phrase means supreme astonishment; the Prophet was not bewildered or disoriented.
rows.anchor: Fahr-i Râzî’nin birinciden sonra kaydettiği bir kavle göre de; “sidre” “râkib”den “rikbe” gibi binâ-i merre olarak Sidre-i Müntehâ hayret-i kusvâ demektir.

rows.speaker: Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: Razi explicitly says the first interpretation, the physical sidra, is the sound one.
rows.anchor: Râzî der ki “sahih olan evvelki vecihtir.”

rows.speaker: Ebussuud
rows.claim: Abu Suud suggests muntaha may mean God, by 53:42, so Sidrat al-Muntaha is God's sidra, as property is attributed to its owner.
rows.anchor: Ebussuud’un kaydettiği bir mânaya göre
